sn35.246:1.1: The same five defilements are listed at [mn151:3.3]().
sn35.246:1.2: “Sorry state” _duhitika_ is from Sanskrit _durhita_ (Rig Veda 8.19.26; Atharva Veda 4.36.9).
sn35.246:3.3: The _ghaṭā_ (“pot”) is the prominent hump of a zebu bull, which is grabbed to this day by bull wranglers.
sn35.246:3.14: For “straightened up”, accept MS reading _udujita_, resolved as _ud_ + √_uj_ + _ita_.
sn35.246:4.1: The “arched harp” (_vīṇa_) was a multi-stringed instrument held in the lap, with the strings attached across a curved open arched neck. It is not the modern Indian instrument called veena, which is a lute or stick zither. Pañcasikha’s harp is described in the same way ([dn21:1.2.4]()), and tradition says they were in fact the same instrument.
sn35.246:4.17: Most of these were established by Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, “The Parts of a Vīnā”, Journal of the American Oriental Society, Vol. 50 (1930), pp. 244–253. “Soundbox” is _doṇi_ (“tub”); “leather soundboard” is _camma_, a piece of leather stretched over the soundbox to enhance the resonance; “neck” is _daṇḍa_, the curved arm or frame; “strings” is _tantiyo_; and “plectrum” is _koṇa_. The remaining part is variously spelled as _upaviṇe_, _upadhiraṇe_, _upadhāraṇe_, or _upaveṇaṁ_, suggesting an early corruption. The preponderance of plural forms nonetheless supports Coomaraswamy’s revised understanding (“The Parts of a Vīṇā”, JAOS, Vol. 57, No. 1 (March 1937), pp. 101–103) that this is Sanskrit _upavīṇa_, _upavāṇa_, or _upaveṇa_ having the sense “bindings”. This would be the “tuning cords” by which the strings are tied to the neck and which also serve for tuning.
sn35.246:4.18: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.9 says you can only catch the sound of a harp by getting hold of the lute or player, using this as a metaphor for the search for the Self. [dn23:19.3]() tells a similar parable, only with a horn. The Upaniṣad has both instruments.
sn35.246:4.24: The rare verb _samanvesati_ is used in [sn4.23:10.4]() and [sn22.87:11.5]() of Māra “searching” for the consciousness of a deceased arahant.
